deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics and is not in Riemann's hand. It is the second page of a letter dated Aachen, 27 October 1875. The writer is Karl Hattendorf, who in 1867 edited Riemann's posthumous paper 'Ueber die Fläche vom kleinsten Inhalt bei gegebener Begrenzung'. The recipient is most likely Heinrich Weber, then preparing Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (1876).

The previous page settles editorial changes to §16 of the minimal-surface paper. That page includes a normalisation: with c-b = 2π/A, the factor sqrt(A(c-b)(β+γ)/(2π)) in du reduces to sqrt(β+γ).

On this page Hattendorf says three things:
(1) He wrote the historical introduction to the 1867 edition last. That was after Riemann's death and, as far as he knows, without Riemann asking for it. It could therefore be replaced by a short note on the date of the investigation and on how the paper reached its present form.
(2) Dating evidence: Riemann spoke to him twice about the problem.
- The first time was probably in the summer vacation of 1861, after Hattendorf had attended Riemann's summer-semester lectures on functions of a complex variable. It was certainly not after summer 1862 ('nach' is underlined). Riemann then said: 'The theory of functions of complex variables admits an interesting application to the problem of minimal surfaces.'
- The second time was in April 1866, when Riemann handed over the manuscript, already as yellowed as it is now. He said: 'I would like this work to be finished. It is, admittedly, already five to six years old.'
(3) Conclusion: Hattendorf dates the manuscript's origin to 1860–1861 (1866 minus 5–6 years).

The next page goes on to describe how the 1867 redaction was produced. Riemann was too ill to speak and communicated by stylus on a slate.

Mathematical content: none on this page. Its significance is as a historical witness. It dates Riemann's treatment of the Plateau problem via complex function theory (and his hypergeometric-type representation of the minimal surface) to 1860–61. That is before the published representations of Enneper (1864) and Weierstrass (1866).
errors: Historical point: the dating rests on Hattendorf's memory and on Riemann's verbal estimate. The inference to 1860–61 is reasonable, but it is testimony rather than documentary proof. It is internally consistent: 1866 minus 5–6 years gives 1860–61, matching the 1861/62 conversation.

results.what: Testimony dating Riemann's work on minimal surfaces (solution of special Plateau problems via complex function theory) to 1860–61, with Riemann's 1861/62 remark that complex function theory applies to minimal surfaces
results.modern_name: Riemann's contribution to the Plateau problem / complex-analytic (Enneper–Weierstrass-type) representation of minimal surfaces
results.usually_credited_to: Enneper (1864) and Weierstrass (1866) for the representation formulas; Riemann's posthumous paper (ed. Hattendorf, 1867) is recognised alongside them

results.what: Editorial history: Hattendorf wrote the historical introduction of the 1867 edition himself after Riemann's death and proposes replacing it with a note on dating and redaction for the Werke
results.modern_name: Editorial provenance of Riemann's Werke text on minimal surfaces

deep.surprise_reason: This is an editor's letter, not Riemann mathematics. The 1860–61 dating and Hattendorf's role in the 1867 redaction are essentially known from the editorial note in Riemann's Werke and from the secondary literature. The exact wording of Riemann's quoted remarks is a minor archival detail.

checkable.sympy: A,c,b,beta,gamma=symbols('A c b beta gamma',positive=True); simplify(sqrt(A*(c-b)*(beta+gamma)/(2*pi)).subs(c, b+2*pi/A) - sqrt(beta+gamma)) == 0
checkable.asserts: The normalisation c-b = 2π/A from the previous page reduces the prefactor of du to sqrt(β+γ).
'Five to six years old' in April 1866 places the manuscript in 1860–1861.

transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image well.
In 'jedenfalls nicht nach dem Sommer 1862' the word 'nach' is underlined in the original.
The quotations are set off with German quotation marks („…“) in the manuscript.
The page is in Hattendorf's hand (a letter of 1875), not Riemann's.
